Norovirus Outbreak Hits Czech Transportation and Logistics Sector, Disrupting Operations

A significant norovirus outbreak has swept through the Czech Republic’s transportation and logistics industry, causing widespread worker absences and site closures as companies scramble to contain the contagion. The outbreak, which began last week in the Ostrava industrial region, has now affected multiple distribution centers and freight hubs across the country, industry sources confirmed on Tuesday.

According to the Czech Association of Transport and Logistics (CATL), at least nine major freight depots and three long-haul trucking companies have reported clusters of illness among staff. Norovirus, a highly contagious virus that causes acute gastroenteritis, typically spreads rapidly in close-contact environments—posing a particular challenge for this sector, where teams work in close quarters and facilities handle high volumes of goods and personnel.

Petr Novak, spokesperson for CATL, stated, “We are seeing absenteeism rates of up to 38 percent in some locations, which is unprecedented for our industry. The health and safety of our workforce is the priority, and affected companies have implemented full sanitation protocols and temporary shutdowns where necessary.”

Several freight terminals in Brno and Plzeň have temporarily closed for deep cleaning after dozens of employees reported symptoms. At the same time, trucking firms have curtailed some routes due to driver shortages. “We have had to suspend or delay more than 60 scheduled deliveries this week alone,” reported Jana Svobodová, operations manager at TransRoute CZ, a national logistics provider. “We are working closely with health authorities, but the situation is evolving hour by hour.”

The outbreak’s impact is already being felt in transit times and capacity constraints. CATL estimates that average delivery delays for shipments originating in affected areas have risen to 36–48 hours. Warehouses are operating with reduced staff, leading to slower order processing and longer turnaround times for cargo.

Analysts warn that if the outbreak continues into next week, the disruption could ripple through the sector’s supply chain. “Every day that hubs operate below capacity increases the backlog,” said Tomas Kral, a logistics analyst at Prague-based consultancy ForwardView. “While contingency plans are in place, the industry’s resilience is being severely tested.”

Health authorities are currently investigating the source of the outbreak and have urged all companies in the sector to reinforce hygiene measures. Industry leaders are calling for government support to ensure rapid testing and minimize operational downtime.

As the situation unfolds, logistics firms and their clients are bracing for continued uncertainty in the critical days ahead.
